cases.title: Fake Income Tax officers put a Navi Mumbai academic under 'digital arrest'
cases.location: Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India; accused from Mumbai and Ahmedabad
cases.channel: phone call, then WhatsApp documents and video calls
steps: The victim got a call from someone posing as an Income Tax officer alleging unpaid tax and a complaint filed in Delhi.
The gang sent forged letters with Income Tax Department, CBI, ED and Supreme Court logos over WhatsApp.
They posed as officials on video calls and told her she was under 'digital arrest'.
Out of fear she shared bank and investment details and transferred money in several payments to six accounts.
The accounts belonged to fake companies the gang had set up.
cases.payment_method: bank transfers to six accounts of fake companies
cases.amount_lost: about Rs 1.81 crore (outlets differ, Rs 1.8 to 2 crore)
cases.outcome: three men arrested by Navi Mumbai Police (reported 3 Jun 2025); others sought
cases.legal_sections: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Information Technology Act (sections not given)
cases.reporting_route: complaint to Navi Mumbai cyber police

cases.title: Couple laundered mailed cash for India-based 'Social Security number' phone scammers
cases.location: South Carolina, USA (couple); prosecuted in Atlanta, Georgia; call centres in India
cases.channel: phone
steps: India-based call centres phoned US residents, including elderly people.
Callers posed as federal agents and claimed the victim's Social Security number was tied to crimes.
They threatened arrest and loss of assets unless the victim sent money.
Victims were told to mail cash to aliases used by network members.
The couple collected the cash and passed it on, laundering over $500,000 from dozens of victims.
cases.payment_method: cash mailed to aliases
cases.amount_lost: over $500,000 from dozens of victims; restitution ordered $320,550 and $259,217
cases.outcome: one defendant sentenced to 2 years 6 months (Dec 2020), the other to 1 year 8 months (Apr 2021)
cases.reporting_route: not reported

cases.title: HMRC investigation: four arrested in London over a multi-million-pound tax phone scam
cases.location: London, UK
cases.channel: phone
steps: Fraudsters phoned UK taxpayers claiming to be from HMRC.
Some were offered a bogus tax refund.
Others were threatened with arrest unless they immediately paid tax bills that did not exist.
Callers also sought personal or bank details, often from elderly or vulnerable people.
cases.payment_method: not reported
cases.amount_lost: not stated for this case; HMRC described a multi-million-pound scam; £10,000 cash seized
cases.outcome: four people arrested on suspicion of money laundering; charge or conviction not found
cases.reporting_route: HMRC online reporting for suspicious calls; Action Fraud

cases.title: RCMP Project OCTAVIA: CRA phone scam, call-centre takedowns in India, money-mule arrests in Brampton
cases.location: Brampton, Ontario, Canada (money mules); call centres in Noida and New Delhi, India
cases.channel: phone
steps: Callers in India posed as Canada Revenue Agency, RCMP or other federal representatives.
They claimed the victim owed unpaid taxes and threatened arrest or imprisonment.
Victims were pressured to pay non-existent fines or taxes, some by mailing cash in envelopes.
Money mules in Canada received the cash, counted it and passed it on to be accessed in India.
cases.payment_method: cash mailed in envelopes to mules in Canada
cases.amount_lost: over $16.8 million reported 2014-2019 (government briefing note); one news report says over $17.2 million
cases.outcome: two Brampton residents charged 12 Feb 2020, a Canada-wide warrant for a third; 39 call centres in Noida and New Delhi taken down with India's CBI; trial outcome not found
cases.legal_sections: fraud over $5,000; laundering proceeds of crime; possession of property obtained by crime
cases.reporting_route: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and local police

cases.title: Adelaide: automated tax-debt warrant call, then fake 'Federal Police' at the door with a card machine
cases.location: Salisbury Downs, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia
cases.channel: automated phone message, then in-person visit
steps: The victim got an automated message saying he had a tax debt and an arrest warrant had been issued.
He suspected a scam, called back and hung up without giving details.
About half an hour later two men in 'Federal Police' jackets came to his door.
They said he owed a tax debt and produced an EFTPOS machine to take payment.
He asked for identification and the men ran off.
cases.payment_method: in-person card payment via EFTPOS terminal (attempted)
cases.amount_lost: none
cases.outcome: SA Police investigating; no arrest reported; the ATO confirmed no debt existed
cases.reporting_route: Crime Stoppers 1800 333 000; ATO and Scamwatch

cases.title: Ahmedabad call centres posing as IRS and USCIS, prosecuted in Houston
cases.location: Ahmedabad, India (call centres); US victims and runner network; prosecuted in Houston, Texas, USA
cases.channel: phone (VoIP, auto-dialers, spoofed IRS caller ID)
steps: Call-centre staff in India used scripts and lead lists to phone US taxpayers and legal immigrants.
Callers posed as IRS or USCIS agents and said the victim owed back taxes or money to the government.
They threatened arrest or deportation unless the victim paid immediately.
Victims were told to buy prepaid cards and read out the serial numbers, or to wire money.
US-based runners cashed out onto reloadable cards under stolen or fake identities and laundered the money, partly via hawala back to India.
quoted_lines: arrest, imprisonment, fines or deportation
cases.payment_method: prepaid and stored-value cards (serial numbers read to the caller), reloadable cards, wire transfers
cases.amount_lost: $61.9 million from 12,469 victims (TIGTA figure, as reported by Journal of Accountancy); restitution ordered $8,970,396
cases.outcome: Oct 2016: 56 individuals and 5 call-centre companies charged; by July 2018 about two dozen US-based defendants sentenced to terms of up to 20 years; Dec 2020: the India-based operator sentenced to 20 years
cases.legal_sections: conspiracy, wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy; 2020 plea also covered identification fraud, access device fraud, and impersonation of a federal officer
cases.reporting_route: TIGTA (800-366-4484) and FTC, per the IRS fact sheet

cases.title: Thane police raid call centres behind fake-IRS calls, later arrest the alleged ringleader
cases.location: Thane and Mumbai, India; victims across the US including Texas
cases.channel: phone, plus fake CP2000 notices by email
steps: Callers phoned US taxpayers, often with limited English, posing as IRS officials.
They threatened that officers would arrive to arrest the victim, or threatened deportation or loss of a licence.
Victims were told to pay a fake tax bill with gift cards, preloaded debit cards or wire transfer.
Some targets also got fake emails with a counterfeit CP2000 form.
A variant asked victims to 'verify' Social Security and bank numbers for a refund.
quoted_lines: Within the next hour, they will be at your doorstep to handcuff and arrest you.
cases.payment_method: gift cards, preloaded debit cards, wire transfers
cases.amount_lost: $44 million from US taxpayers and 742 victims in Texas alone (KSAT); one Texas victim paid over $5,000 in gift cards
cases.outcome: 70 arrested and 600 questioned in the Oct 2016 raids; the alleged ringleader arrested at Mumbai airport on 8 Apr 2017
cases.reporting_route: hang up and call the IRS directly; TIGTA or FTC

cases.title: Singapore: fake police caller says victim's identity misused in money laundering; cash and gold collected by an 'agent' (suspect arrested, to be charged)
cases.location: Victim in the Kovan area, Singapore; suspect a Malaysian national arrested in Singapore while trying to leave; scam run by a transnational syndicate per police
steps: Caller claimed to be a police officer and said the victim's identity had been misused in money laundering.
Victim was told to give banking and personal information and not to tell anyone, including family, about the 'investigation'.
Victim was told to withdraw cash and hand it and gold to an 'agent' for 'investigation purposes'.
A 34-year-old Malaysian woman, tasked by unknown persons, collected the cash and gold; she was arrested on 19 May 2026 and two gold bars were seized.
Police said she was to be charged in court on 21 May 2026.
cases.channel: phone call
cases.amount_lost: $13,700 in cash plus gold items (gold quantity not stated; currency symbol as reported)
cases.payment_method: cash and gold handed to an 'agent' in person
cases.legal_sections: Section 51, Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (assisting another to retain benefits from criminal conduct); max 10 years' jail, fine up to $500,000, or both
cases.outcome: Suspect arrested 19 May 2026; to be charged in court 21 May 2026 (no verdict reported)
cases.reporting_route: Victim reported to police. Police advise the Police Hotline 1800-255-0000, police.gov.sg/i-witness, 999 for urgent help, and the ScamShield Helpline 1799 if unsure.
quoted_lines: investigation purposes
prove her innocence

cases.title: Singapore: fake bank caller transferred to fake MHA officer who alleges money laundering and shows fake arrest warrant; victims pay or hand over gold
cases.location: Singapore
steps: Victim gets an unsolicited call from a scammer posing as a bank representative, who says a credit card under their name was found or used for transactions.
If the victim denies it, the call is transferred to a scammer posing as an MHA officer.
The MHA impersonator alleges the victim is involved in crimes such as money laundering.
In some cases the scammers present fake official documents: a warrant of arrest, a notice of investigation and a court hearing appointment.
Victims are told to make transactions 'for investigation purposes' (PayNow, gold or valuables to unknown persons, crypto-related transfers).
Victims realise it is a scam when the scammers become uncontactable.
cases.channel: phone call (fake documents also shown; delivery method not stated)
cases.amount_lost: about $52,000 across at least 7 cases since September 2025 (currency symbol as written in the advisory)
cases.payment_method: PayNow transfers (including scanning a YouTrip QR code), gold or other valuables handed to unknown persons, cryptocurrency-related transfers
cases.outcome: Police advisory only; no arrests or prosecution reported
cases.reporting_route: Call your bank immediately to report and block fraudulent transactions, then make a police report; ScamShield Helpline 1799 or the ScamShield app if unsure
quoted_lines: will never do the following over a phone call

cases.title: England: two men convicted over fake-police phone fraud on elderly landline users (covert-investigation pretext; adjacent, no fine or warrant reported)
cases.location: Victims in Thames Valley and elsewhere in England (Pangbourne, Reading, Thame, Oxford, Wallingford, Wokingham, Naphill, Hereford, Leicestershire, West Sussex); sentenced at Reading Crown Court
steps: Callers posed as police officers using two fictional officer identities.
Victims were told to hang up and dial 999, but the callers kept the line open so victims believed they were speaking to another officer.
Callers said the money would help expose fraud within financial institutions or support fictional covert operations.
Victims were pressured over hours (60 hours of calls in total, one victim kept on the phone for eight hours) to withdraw cash and hand it over.
Two men were convicted of conspiracy to commit fraud, one by guilty plea and one by jury after a six-day trial.
cases.channel: phone call (landline)
cases.amount_lost: GBP 87,000 requested from 17 victims aged 69-87; GBP 9,000 reached the criminals after police intervention
cases.payment_method: cash withdrawn by victims and handed over
cases.outcome: One defendant (guilty plea) sentenced to 1 year 9 months, 3 years total with activated earlier sentences; the other (convicted by jury) sentenced to 2 years
cases.reporting_route: not reported (article gives only general caution about unsolicited calls)
quoted_lines: neither the police nor your bank will ever ask you for money

cases.title: Singapore: five arrested over China Officials Impersonation Scam couriers with fake police, Chinese Police and Interpol papers (plus a separate internet love scam)
cases.location: Singapore (arrests 11-17 May 2021; release dated 20 May 2021)
steps: Scammers posed as China officials and told victims their credit or debit card details were used in fraudulent transactions, or that their bank accounts were involved in money laundering.
Victims were deceived into handing over money for purported investigations and disclosing banking details, including one-time passwords.

Two men and two women, aged 18-51, allegedly acted on the scammers' instructions and met victims to deliver purported 'official investigation documents', using fake ID claiming to be Singapore Police Force, Chinese Police or Interpol.
Police seized a fake SPF warrant card, a China Police pass, an Interpol pass and fake investigation documents.
Five people in total (two women, three men) were arrested; one 31-year-old man was believed to be an unlicensed remittance agent.
cases.channel: not reported (initial contact channel is not stated)
cases.amount_lost: over S$200,000 across four China Officials Impersonation cases; separate internet love scam: S$1,600 in one report, over S$4,000 alleged in total
cases.payment_method: money handed over for 'investigations' and banking details/OTPs disclosed; transfer method not specified
cases.legal_sections: Possible offences cited: Penal Code s420 (cheating), s170 (impersonating a public servant); Payment Services Act 2019 s5 (unlicensed payment services)
cases.outcome: Five arrested; police investigations ongoing; no charges, conviction or sentence reported
cases.reporting_route: not reported

cases.title: Retired Bhopal woman defrauded of Rs 25.65 lakh after video call from fake counter-terrorism officer
cases.location: Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, India
cases.channel: Video call, then a call from a person posing as an officer of the Internal Security and Counter Terrorism Department (channel of second call not stated)
cases.amount_lost: Rs 25.65 lakh (Rs 16.50 lakh on 6 Nov and Rs 9.15 lakh on 7 Nov)
cases.payment_method: Deposits into specified bank accounts (no account details given)
cases.reporting_route: Victim complained to cyber police on 28 Nov (year not stated in the article); CBI Bhopal later registered a regular case against unknown suspects after a Supreme Court suo motu matter
cases.outcome: No arrests reported; case against unknown suspects; investigation handed to the Anti-Corruption Bureau, Bhopal
steps: On 4 Nov 2024 the victim, a 64-year-old retired irrigation department employee, got a video call saying a complaint had been filed against her
A person posing as an officer of the Internal Security and Counter Terrorism Department said her account funds were used for terrorism
She was threatened with legal action and property seizure and shown a forged seizure order
She deposited Rs 16.50 lakh on 6 Nov and Rs 9.15 lakh on 7 Nov into specified accounts
CBI Bhopal registered a case against unknown suspects and the probe went to the ACB

cases.title: Delhi retired government officer kept on WhatsApp video calls for 72+ hours, loses Rs 48.5 lakh
cases.location: New Delhi, India (South West Delhi Police Cyber Crime Cell)
cases.channel: WhatsApp calls, including continuous video calls
cases.amount_lost: Rs 48.5 lakh, after liquidating fixed deposits, PPF and other savings
cases.payment_method: Transfers to current accounts of shell companies, which scammers claimed were under Supreme Court supervision
cases.reporting_route: Case handled by South West Delhi Police Cyber Crime Cell; linked to 28 complaints logged on the national cybercrime reporting portal
cases.outcome: Three arrested; three smartphones and documents recovered; shell companies reportedly linked to Chinese operators and Hong Kong-based IP addresses; no court outcome reported
steps: On 2 March 2025 a WhatsApp caller posing as TRAI said a money-laundering case in Mumbai was filed under his Aadhaar
He was passed to a fake Mumbai Police sub-inspector, then a fake CBI chief and a fake Supreme Court judge
He was kept on continuous video calls for over 72 hours and barred from contacting anyone
Mock virtual court proceedings pressured him to liquidate FDs, PPF and savings
He paid Rs 48.5 lakh to accounts said to be under Supreme Court supervision
Police arrested three people and mapped account operators, tech handlers and recruiters

cases.title: Hyderabad police arrest three in digital arrest fraud on 71-year-old man
cases.location: Hyderabad, Telangana, India
cases.channel: Video call from callers posing as CBI officials (first contact not described)
cases.amount_lost: Rs 1,92,50,070 (about Rs 1.93 crore)
cases.payment_method: Deposits into multiple bank accounts
cases.reporting_route: Victim approached Hyderabad cybercrime police, who registered a case
cases.outcome: Three arrested (a 24-year-old student and two businessmen in their mid-40s); prime accused absconding; the three linked to five cases across India, two in Telangana. Police said agencies never demand money to avoid arrest and arrests are never made over video calls
steps: Callers posing as CBI said a bank account opened with the victim's Aadhaar was linked to a criminal case
On a video call they showed him an ATM card in his name
They sent a fake FIR attributed to the Delhi Crime Branch
They demanded money to 'clear the issue'; he deposited about Rs 1.93 crore into multiple accounts between 7 and 14 Nov
Police arrested three suspects; the prime accused remains at large

cases.title: Gandhinagar cyber centre arrests alleged key financial operator of network linked to 1,090 cases and over Rs 1,071 crore in digital arrest fraud
cases.date: 2026-08-17 (article date; dates of the individual frauds not reported)
cases.location: Gandhinagar, Gujarat, India (victims across India); the accused was arrested in Barpeta, Assam
cases.channel: Video calls from callers posing as police officials (first contact not described)
cases.amount_lost: Network linked by police to 1,090 cybercrime cases and more than Rs 1,071 crore (exact figure Rs 10,71,55,66,034); no per-victim amount
cases.payment_method: Transfers to multiple bank accounts after victims shared bank details; proceeds converted to cryptocurrency and passed to members of a Chinese network (police statement)
cases.reporting_route: A senior citizen's case led the Gandhinagar cyber centre to start a technical investigation; police also visited potential victims' homes to stop further fraud
cases.outcome: One alleged key financial operator arrested and being questioned; no charges, court proceedings or bail reported; police urged people not to panic if an agency threatens arrest on a video call
steps: Gang posed as police officials and used forged Supreme Court letters to scare victims
Victims were told serious criminal cases were registered against them
Victims were placed under so-called digital arrest through video calls
Victims were pressured to share bank details and send money to multiple accounts
A senior citizen's case led police to find about 10 similar cases running at the same time
Police arrested one alleged financial operator; proceeds had been converted to crypto and sent to a Chinese network

cases.title: Retired Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board employee kept on video calls for three days, loses Rs 3 lakh
cases.location: Kolar area, Bhopal (state capital), Madhya Pradesh, India
cases.channel: WhatsApp video call from a caller dressed like a law enforcement officer, then continuous video calls and messages
cases.amount_lost: Rs 3 lakh
cases.payment_method: RTGS from his bank to a 'Government Clearance Account' number supplied by the scammers
cases.legal_sections: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and IT Act (specific sections not stated), FIR against unidentified suspects
cases.reporting_route: Reported to Kolar police station; FIR registered
cases.outcome: No arrests; police tracing the WhatsApp numbers and the receiving bank account; victim realised the fraud when more money was demanded
steps: Caller posing as a CBI sub-inspector said the victim's SIM card was used in a high-profile financial scam
He was told he was under digital arrest and accused of money laundering
He was warned of arrest if he contacted family or local police
He was kept on continuous video calls and messages for three days
On 8 Jan he sent Rs 3 lakh by RTGS to a Government Clearance Account to 'verify his funds'
He reported it when more money was demanded; the SHO said India has no legal provision for digital arrest

cases.title: Gujarat cyber crime branch arrests 17 in digital arrest racket, including four Taiwanese nationals
cases.date: 2024-10-14 (article date); complaint received the previous month per police; arrest dates not given
cases.location: Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India (raids in Gujarat, Delhi, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Odisha, Maharashtra)
cases.channel: Video or audio calls from call centres made to look like investigative agency offices
cases.amount_lost: A senior citizen deposited Rs 79.34 lakh; police believe about 1,000 people may have been targeted
cases.payment_method: Transfers to other bank accounts and crypto accounts in Dubai; accused earned hawala commissions
cases.reporting_route: Senior citizen registered a complaint, followed by a cyber crime branch operation
cases.outcome: 17 arrested (four Taiwanese nationals and 13 from Gujarat, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Odisha, Rajasthan); seized Rs 12.75 lakh cash, 761 SIM cards, 120 phones, 96 cheque books, 92 debit/credit cards, 42 passbooks; no charges or court outcome reported
steps: Victims were told by callers posing as TRAI, CBI and cybercrime branch officials that their accounts were used for illegal transactions
Victims were kept under watch through video or audio calls
One senior citizen was digitally arrested for 10 days and deposited Rs 79.34 lakh as 'refundable' fees to resolve an 'RBI issue'
Money was routed to other accounts and Dubai crypto accounts
Police arrested 17, including four Taiwanese who provided the gang's app with wallet integration

cases.title: Bengaluru software engineer held under digital arrest for over six months, loses about Rs 31.83 crore
cases.location: Indiranagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India
cases.channel: Phone call from a fake courier (DHL) caller, transferred to fake CBI officers, then constant Skype video surveillance
cases.amount_lost: About Rs 31.83 crore (article text says about Rs 32 crore) across 187 bank transfers
cases.payment_method: Bank transfers
cases.reporting_route: Victim complained; a case was registered (details not given)
cases.outcome: Case registered; no arrests mentioned; ordeal ended when the fraudsters sent a 'clearance letter'
quoted_lines: all evidence is against you
steps: On 15 Sept 2024 a caller claiming to be from a courier firm said a parcel in her name held credit cards, passports and MDMA
The call was passed to people posing as CBI officers who threatened her
She was kept under constant Skype video watch, told not to contact police and that criminals were watching her home
Fraudsters told her to verify her assets with the RBI's Financial Intelligence Unit and gave forged letters
She made 187 bank transfers over more than six months
A 'clearance letter' from the fraudsters ended it; a case was registered

cases.title: Fake FedEx and Mumbai cyber police callers, claiming a Taiwan-bound parcel held drugs and Aadhaar, take Rs 5.79 lakh from an actor
cases.location: Mumbai, Maharashtra, India (complaint at DN Nagar police station)
cases.channel: phone call
steps: A caller claiming to be a FedEx employee said a package in her name, bound for Taiwan, was seized by customs for containing drugs and that her Aadhaar card was inside.
A second caller posing as a Mumbai cyber police officer said her Aadhaar was linked to three bank accounts in a money-laundering case.
He demanded Rs 96,525 to 'prove innocence', and she was told to transfer Rs 4,83,291 to a Punjab National Bank account to avoid legal trouble.
A few days later she told her landlord about the calls and realised she had been scammed.
cases.amount_lost: Rs 5.79 lakh (as reported)
cases.payment_method: bank transfer to a Punjab National Bank account (the article does not say clearly how the two sums were paid)
cases.outcome: Case registered at DN Nagar police station and investigation ongoing at publication. No arrests or recovery reported. FedEx issued a statement warning customers about such calls (wording not given).
cases.reporting_route: police complaint at DN Nagar police station, Mumbai

cases.title: Fake FedEx, customs and Mumbai police callers over Skype and WhatsApp take about Rs 1 crore from a Bengaluru software engineer
cases.location: Bengaluru, Karnataka, India
cases.channel: Skype call, then WhatsApp
steps: On May 16, a caller on Skype posing as a FedEx logistics executive said a parcel in her name, sent from Mumbai airport to Taiwan, held about 200 g of narcotics and several passports.
A caller posing as a Customs officer said a case had been filed under the NDPS Act; she was told to take the call from an isolated room and her Aadhaar details were collected.
She was connected to a person claiming to be Mumbai Police, who ran a staged interrogation; she had to keep her camera on while the callers hid their faces.
She was told to transfer money to an account said to belong to the Reserve Bank of India, for 'verification'.
On May 17, callers on WhatsApp asked for transfers of Rs 16 lakh, then Rs 75 lakh and Rs 9.8 lakh, promising a refund within 30 days; she filed a police complaint on May 18.
cases.amount_lost: about Rs 1 crore over two days (as reported)
cases.payment_method: bank transfers to account numbers supplied by the callers (said to belong to the RBI)
cases.outcome: Police complaint filed on 2024-05-18. The article reports no arrests, FIR details, investigation progress or recovery.
cases.reporting_route: police complaint
cases.legal_sections: not reported (the fake officer claimed an NDPS Act case; no section given)

cases.title: Fake FedEx Mumbai and Mumbai police callers, with Skype video call, take Rs 15.26 lakh from a Chennai resident over a 'contraband parcel to Taiwan'
cases.location: Kilpauk, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India (victim); suspect arrested in Rajasthan (from Daulatpura near Jaipur)
cases.channel: phone call, then Skype call
steps: On March 17, a caller claiming to be from FedEx Mumbai said a parcel the victim had sent from Mumbai to Taiwan contained contraband.
The call was transferred to a person posing as a Mumbai police official, who threatened him with arrest.
Over a Skype call, the victim was told to transfer his bank balance to a specified account; he was told the money would go to the RBI and be returned if he was found not guilty.
He made two bank transfers totalling Rs 15.26 lakh, then realised the fraud after visiting his bank and filed a police complaint.
A Chennai cybercrime team went to Rajasthan and arrested a 23-year-old suspect; he was produced before a court in Rajasthan, then brought to Chennai, produced in court again and lodged in prison.
cases.amount_lost: Rs 15.26 lakh (as reported)
cases.payment_method: bank transfers in two instalments to an account specified by the fraudsters
cases.outcome: A 23-year-old suspect was arrested in Rajasthan by Chennai cybercrime police, produced before a court there, then brought to Chennai and lodged in prison after a court appearance. No recovery or conviction reported. The same article says Chennai police arrested five men in April in a similar case.
cases.reporting_route: victim visited his bank, then filed a police complaint (Chennai cybercrime police)

cases.title: UK police arrest eight men over scam texts including Royal Mail missed-delivery fee smishing
cases.location: Birmingham, Coventry, London and Colchester, England, UK
cases.channel: SMS text
steps: Texts claimed a Royal Mail parcel was awaiting delivery and asked for a GBP 1.99 settlement fee via a link.
The link led to a site made to look like the official Royal Mail site, asking for personal and payment details.
Specialist unit DCPCU (City of London and Metropolitan Police) made dawn arrests of eight men across the Midlands and South of England, part of a week of action on scam messages.
A man from Enfield, London, was charged with three offences and was due at Inner London Crown Court on 21 June 2021.
The other seven were released under investigation.
cases.amount_lost: not reported
cases.payment_method: GBP 1.99 fee via link; card and personal details harvested
cases.outcome: One man charged with three offences; seven released under investigation; no conviction reported. Royal Mail says it never sends texts and uses a grey card for fees due.

cases.legal_sections: fraud by false representation; possession of articles for use in fraud; possession of criminal property (money laundering)

cases.title: Virtual kidnapping of an international student in Canberra via fake Chinese police 'arrest'; man charged
cases.location: Canberra, ACT, Australia (accused had been living in Queensland and was extradited)
steps: From August 2023 a man allegedly posed as a Chinese police officer investigating the student for money laundering.
She was pressured to keep the contact secret and persuaded to check into a hotel, where he allegedly 'arrested' her.
He demanded 'bail' payments, which she paid that day and over the following weeks.
She was convinced to hand over her phone and social media accounts and to book another hotel.
He allegedly contacted her family overseas, claimed she had been kidnapped and demanded a ransom.
Family and friends reported her missing to ACT Policing, and she was found at a Belconnen hotel.
Police identified him from CCTV, traced him to Queensland and he was extradited to the ACT.
cases.channel: Not reported for first contact (article does not say phone, app or message); in-person hotel 'arrest' followed

cases.payment_method: not reported
cases.reporting_route: Family and friends reported her missing to ACT Policing, which investigated

cases.legal_sections: Charges named only as unlawfully confining a person and impersonating a police officer; no statute sections given

cases.title: Sydney student persuaded to fake her own kidnapping; family in China pays over $200,000
cases.location: Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (family in China)
steps: In July the student received an email purporting to be from Chinese police saying her personal details were used on a package intercepted overseas.
The scam evolved into a 'virtual kidnapping', and the student was convinced to fake her own kidnapping.
On 8 September friends reported her missing to police.
Videos and images of her, apparently held at an unknown location, were sent to her family in China via WeChat.

cases.title: Hong Kong: five arrested over ten 'bail' and compensation scams on retirees
cases.location: Hong Kong (police operation 6-8 Nov 2025); mainland-based key member on a two-way permit supervised handovers
steps: Fraudsters impersonated the victims' children or the children's friends.
They claimed an arrest requiring bail, or compensation owed for bodily harm to someone.
Retirees aged 67 to 93 were told to hand large sums of cash to strangers.
Money mules collected the cash; one or two key members (often mainlanders on brief stays) supervised, and the mules' ID cards were held and photographed on handover day.
Key members deposited the money into the syndicate's cryptocurrency account.
Police arrested five people aged 16 to 34 over ten scams.

cases.channel: phone (article calls it a 'cross-boundary phone scam syndicate'; first contact not described)
cases.payment_method: cash handed to strangers (money mules), passed to key members who deposited it into the syndicate's cryptocurrency account

cases.reporting_route: not reported

cases.title: Vermont-led federal indictment: 25 Canadian nationals charged over nationwide 'grandparent scam'
cases.location: District of Vermont, USA (victims in Vermont and 40+ other states); call centres in and around Montreal, Quebec, Canada
steps: From summer 2021 to June 2024, callers at call centres near Montreal phoned elderly Americans.
They posed as a relative, typically a grandchild, arrested after a car crash and needing bail; others posed as an attorney.
Victims were told a gag order barred them from telling anyone.
A person falsely posing as a bail bondsman came to the victim's home to collect the cash.
Money was sent to Canada via cash deliveries and transactions, sometimes crypto.
On 4 June 2024 Canadian police searched call centres and found many defendants calling victims in Virginia; the 25-defendant indictment was announced 4 Mar 2025.
cases.amount_lost: more than $21 million from elderly Americans
cases.channel: phone call
cases.payment_method: cash collected from victims' homes by someone posing as a bail bondsman; money moved to Canada by cash deliveries and financial transactions, sometimes involving cryptocurrency
cases.outcome: Grand jury indictment returned 20 Feb 2025, announced 4 Mar 2025; all but two of 25 arrested in Canada on 4 Mar 2025; two at large. Nine others were charged earlier in the same district. Allegations only; no convictions reported.
cases.reporting_route: DOJ National Elder Fraud Hotline (833-FRAUD-11), for victims aged 60+
cases.legal_sections: Indictment charges 'participation in a grandparent scam' (no statute named in release). Five alleged call-centre managers also charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering (up to 40 years); the rest face up to 20 years.

cases.title: Two young people in Singapore staged as hostages; videos sent to parents in China to demand ransom
cases.location: Singapore (victims in Singapore; parents in China; callers posed as Chinese police)
cases.channel: unsolicited phone call from a caller posing as an immigration (ICA) officer, transferred to a caller posing as Chinese police, then messages and video calls on the victims' phones
steps: Each victim got an unsolicited call supposedly from an immigration officer, then was transferred to a caller posing as a Chinese police officer, starting around late October or early November 2023.
The callers accused them of money laundering and said they must pay bail to avoid arrest or deportation.
Victims had to report in several times a day by video call or messages and transferred money to accounts the callers gave.
In early January 2024 they were told to record themselves tied up and pretending to be captured, framed as scam awareness material; a suspect pointed a knife at the woman during filming.

The scammers sent the videos to the victims' parents in China to demand ransom, without the victims knowing; the parents alerted friends in Singapore, who reported to police on 2024-01-17.

cases.reporting_route: Members of the local group complained to the Erie County Sheriff's Office about suspected fraud by another member. Prosecuted by the Erie County District Attorney's Office.
cases.legal_sections: Grand Larceny 3rd degree (Class D felony, up to 7 years) at arraignment. Reduced to Petit Larceny (Class A misdemeanor) on the plea.
cases.outcome: Released on own recognizance at arraignment. Pleaded guilty on 2025-11-19 to one count of Petit Larceny, with $1,600 restitution paid as a condition of the plea. Sentencing was set for 2026-02-03 at 9:30 am (maximum 364 days in jail). The sentence is not reported in the opened sources.
steps: A local group ran a social media fundraiser for Hurricane Helene relief (offense dates on or about 2024-09-27 to 2024-10-04).
Members of the group complained to the Sheriff's Office that another member had defrauded it. The investigation began in October 2024.
Donated money was moved from a PayPal account to the defendant's personal bank account and spent on unauthorized personal expenses.
The defendant was arraigned on 2025-01-22 for grand larceny, alleged to be over $5,000.
On 2025-11-19 the defendant pleaded guilty to petit larceny. The release puts the amount at $1,600, repaid in full.

sources.outlet: Erie County District Attorney's Office, press release (arraignment)
Erie County District Attorney's Office, press release (plea)

cases.title: Man posing as a member of a wealthy rum-company family got businesses and celebrities to collect Hurricane Maria donations, then paid vendors with bad checks
cases.location: South Florida, USA (defendant fled in late 2017). Arrested in Brooklyn, New York, in January 2018. Aid destined for Puerto Rico.
cases.channel: not stated; he persuaded business owners, activists and celebrities to collect donations
cases.amount_lost: not reported. More than $500,000 in fraudulent checks was issued, for warehouse space and cargo plane charters. This is not a stated donor loss.
cases.payment_method: Fraudulent checks to warehouse and charter-plane vendors
cases.reporting_route: not reported
cases.legal_sections: Wire fraud (one count, by guilty plea; maximum 20 years)
cases.outcome: Pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries up to 20 years. At least some donations were shipped to Puerto Rico, but it is unclear whether the aid reached storm victims. No sentence reported. He also had an outstanding Orlando arrest warrant for violating probation in a separate fraud case.
steps: The defendant posed as a member of the family that owns a Puerto Rican rum maker.
He convinced business owners, activists and celebrities to collect Hurricane Maria donations, promising to pay to ship them to Puerto Rico.
He issued fraudulent checks, totalling over $500,000, for warehouse space and charter cargo planes.
When the companies demanded cash, he claimed he was abroad dealing with the death of a daughter who did not exist.
He fled South Florida in late 2017, was arrested in Brooklyn in January 2018, and pleaded guilty to wire fraud in April 2018.

sources.outlet: Constantine LLP (formerly Constantine Cannon), Whistleblower Group blog, 'Fraudster of the Week'

cases.title: Friend who offered to recover crypto-scam losses charged with cheating in Singapore
cases.location: Singapore (Clementi Police Division)
cases.channel: personal contact: a friend the victim confided in
steps: A 69-year-old man lost money in a cryptocurrency scam and told a friend.
Over about 15 months, the friend, aged 43, asked for payments labelled legal fees, witness protection fees and other administrative fees.
He asked for more on the claim the matter could be heard in overseas courts.
The victim made multiple transfers, at least S$186,000 in total.
Police got a report on 27 Sep 2026 and arrested the suspect on 21 Oct 2026.
cases.payment_method: multiple transfers (type not specified)
cases.amount_lost: at least S$186,000
cases.outcome: arrested; to be charged in court on 23 Oct 2026 (allegations, no conviction)
cases.reporting_route: police report

cases.title: Kharkiv call centre promised older fraud victims recovery of lost funds, Eurojust action
cases.location: Latvia (victims) and Ukraine (call centre in Kharkiv)
cases.channel: phone call centre targeting people already defrauded
steps: An organised group targeted older people who had already been defrauded.
Operators falsely promised to recover their lost funds and took more money from them.
They also pitched fake investments, including crypto, with fabricated profit reports, and set up credit agreements without victims' knowledge.
Victims in Latvia reported it, and investigators traced the network to Ukraine.
A joint investigation team was set up through Eurojust in April 2026.
quoted_lines: falsely promised to recover lost funds
cases.payment_method: not reported
cases.amount_lost: hundreds of thousands of euros
cases.outcome: four leaders arrested and five more identified as suspects on 26 May 2026; 14 searches; no convictions yet
cases.reporting_route: victims reported to Latvian authorities

cases.title: Tirana call centres re-contacted fraud victims with a recovery offer, Eurojust action
cases.location: Austria (victims) and Albania (call centres in Tirana)
cases.channel: phone call centres working in German, English, Italian, Greek and Spanish
steps: Austrian authorities opened an investigation after many victims were reported in Vienna around June 2023.
The network ran call centres in Tirana selling false investment opportunities.
Operators contacted people who had already lost money through fraudulent platforms and offered to help recover it.
Those who responded were told to open crypto accounts and make an initial EUR 500 deposit, which the offenders aimed to take.
Austria and Albania formed a joint investigation team with Eurojust and Europol support.
cases.payment_method: initial EUR 500 deposit via cryptocurrency accounts
cases.amount_lost: estimated over EUR 50 million for the whole network, not only the recovery offers
cases.outcome: 10 arrested in Tirana; 3 call centres and 9 homes searched; EUR 891,735 seized; no convictions yet
cases.reporting_route: not reported

cases.title: Syndicate posing as Malaysia's National Scam Response Centre sold fake fund recovery
cases.location: Malaysia (Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Johor, Terengganu)
cases.channel: Facebook ads, then WhatsApp
steps: Victims saw advertisements on Facebook.
Suspects contacted them on WhatsApp claiming to represent the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC).
They offered to recover money lost to earlier scams but required upfront payment.
Victims paid several times into different bank accounts.
More payments were requested and no refund came; most victims had been scammed before.
cases.payment_method: bank transfers to multiple accounts
cases.amount_lost: RM68,491 across six cases
cases.outcome: police warning from Bukit Aman Commercial Crime Investigation Department; no arrests reported
cases.reporting_route: NSRC 997; police report at the nearest station

cases.title: Dnipro call centre sold crypto frauds, then offered to recover lost assets for a fee, Eurojust action
cases.location: Latvia and Lithuania (victims) and Ukraine (call centre in Dnipro)
cases.channel: call centre; remote-access software used on investment victims
steps: The call centre sold fake crypto investments.
Staff used remote-access software to move victims' funds to group-controlled wallets.
The group then targeted existing victims again, offering to help recover lost assets.
It asked for payment for 'legal support to return lost assets'.
Victims in Latvia and Lithuania reported it, and Eurojust set up a joint investigation team.
quoted_lines: legal support to return lost assets
cases.payment_method: not reported
cases.amount_lost: over EUR 160,000 for known victims in Latvia and Lithuania (whole operation)
cases.outcome: 11 arrested; 32 locations searched; EUR 400,000 cash and two crypto wallets seized; no convictions yet
cases.reporting_route: not reported

cases.title: Impostor of the 1930 cyber helpline arrested in Mumbai for charging fraud victims to recover money
cases.location: Mumbai / Panvel, Navi Mumbai, India
cases.channel: WhatsApp (ID card sent as proof); contacted people already defrauded online
steps: The accused targeted people who had already lost money in online fraud.
He posed as a member of the 1930 cyber helpline and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.
He offered to help victims recover their lost money.
He sent his identity card over WhatsApp to look legitimate.
He asked for money, citing court-related work and lawyers' fees.
Victims paid into his bank account and UPI number; several complained to West Region Cyber Police Station, Mumbai.
cases.payment_method: Bank transfer and UPI to the accused's own account
cases.amount_lost: not reported; police received several complaints
cases.outcome: Arrested by West Region Cyber Police Station, Mumbai (PTI, 11 Jul 2025); charge outcome not reported
cases.legal_sections: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Information Technology Act, for impersonation and cheating (sections not given)
cases.reporting_route: complaints to West Region Cyber Police Station, Mumbai

advisories.body: FTC Consumer Alert 'Giving wisely in the wake of natural disasters' by an FTC Consumer Education Specialist.
advisories.says: Be wary of charities that appeared suddenly after a news event; don't assume charity posts on social media are legitimate.
advisories.reporting_route: None in the article text. The page's site navigation links to ReportFraud.ftc.gov, but the article does not tell readers to report there.

advisories.body: Royal Cayman Islands Police Service and Cayman Islands Government warning about texts posing as the postal service, saying a parcel is held until customs duties are paid, with links to a fake government-style payment site.
advisories.says: The Cayman Islands Government entities will never ask you to pay customs duties or fees via text message.
advisories.reporting_route: Contact your bank if you clicked a link or entered payment details; report to the Royal Cayman Islands Police Service on 949-4222 (+1 345 949-4222).

advisories.body: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) public advisory issued Saturday 5 October 2024, reported by ETV Bharat on 6 October 2024 (the report opened; the I4C page itself was not opened). Reporting: helpline 1930 or www.cybercrime.gov.in.
advisories.says: CBI/Police/Custom/ED/Judges DO NOT arrest you on video call.
advisories.reporting_route: Helpline 1930 or www.cybercrime.gov.in

advisories.body: CBI alert on digital arrest fraud, reported by Free Press Journal on 19 April 2026. It warns that scammers falsely invoke digital arrest in the CBI's name, make video calls in police uniform, threaten arrest and ask for money. It advises staying calm, not sharing personal or financial details, blocking the number and contacting police. No helpline is named.
advisories.says: The police never make video calls to place anyone under arrest.
advisories.reporting_route: Block the number and approach the police; no helpline named

advisories.body: FBI IC3 PSA I-010324-PSA, 3 January 2024. Scammers spoof numbers to appear as a mobile carrier, large retailer, delivery service or the Chinese Embassy/Consulate, claiming the victim's information is tied to a financial fraud investigation. The call moves to a fake Chinese provincial police officer who shows forged credentials and threatens arrest. Victims are told to accept 24/7 video and audio monitoring and to wire a large sum to a Chinese bank account to prove innocence or post bail. Some are pushed to borrow money, act as money mules or recruit other students. Targets are the US Chinese community, especially students.
advisories.says: Contact from a seemingly official phone number is not proof of official action.
advisories.reporting_route: IC3 (www.ic3.gov) with wire instructions, phone numbers and messages; local FBI field office; your bank or payment provider immediately; campus security.

advisories.body: FBI IC3 PSA I-041023-PSA, 10 April 2023. Scammers pose as Chinese law enforcement or prosecutors, often by phone with spoofed numbers tied to China's Ministry of Public Security, a local Public Security Bureau or a US-based Chinese Consulate, and sometimes via messaging apps. They claim the victim is a suspect in a financial crime and may send forged arrest warrants. They threaten arrest or violence unless the victim pays. The PSA gives no payment amounts or methods.
advisories.says: Contact from an apparently official phone number is not proof of official action.
advisories.reporting_route: IC3 (www.ic3.gov); local FBI field office (www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices).

advisories.body: Report on a Better Business Bureau warning (WSBT 22 reporter, published on OKCFOX) that scammers create fake customer service numbers that appear in voice-search results. Red flags: caller redirects to a website designed to steal information or says they cannot help without payment. Advice: verify numbers, use the official app or website, pay by credit card.
advisories.says: Scammers are creating fake customer service numbers that will appear in search results when you use search by voice.
advisories.reporting_route: BBB Scam Tracker (bbb.org/scamtracker/reportscam). Quote and route confirmed; article updated 2023-11-04.

advisories.body: US Federal Trade Commission consumer alert on missed jury duty payment scams
advisories.says: Courts never ask for immediate payment over the phone.
advisories.reporting_route: ReportFraud.ftc.gov

advisories.body: US District Court, Middle District of Louisiana, posting a U.S. Marshals Service warning on fake jury-duty warrant calls
advisories.says: should not provide any personal identification or money to the caller
advisories.reporting_route: local U.S. Marshals Service office or local FBI office

advisories.body: US District Court, Northern District of Indiana notice on fake arrest warrants for jury duty
advisories.says: neither it nor any law enforcement agency will email or call to request fine payments (paraphrase; the page says fines are imposed by a judge in open court)
advisories.reporting_route: FTC (reportfraud.ftc.gov); court Clerk's Office at 877-377-1219 to report possible juror fraud

advisories.body: Internal Revenue Service (FS-2017-7, archived)
advisories.says: The IRS starts most contact by mail; scam callers demand immediate payment by prepaid card, gift card or wire and threaten arrest.
advisories.reporting_route: TIGTA 800-366-4484; FTC Complaint Assistant; phishing@irs.gov

advisories.body: Canada Revenue Agency (Recognize a scam)
advisories.says: The CRA won't demand payment by e-transfer, crypto, prepaid or gift cards, and won't threaten to deport or arrest you.
advisories.reporting_route: CRA scam report page, local police, Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre

advisories.body: HM Revenue and Customs (reporting suspicious HMRC contact)
advisories.says: HMRC offers an online service to report a suspicious HMRC phone call and lists its genuine contacts to check against.
advisories.reporting_route: HMRC online 'Report a suspicious HMRC phone call' service

advisories.body: FBI IC3 public service announcement on criminals using generative AI, including voice cloning in family-crisis or emergency calls.
advisories.says: Criminals generate short audio clips containing a loved one's voice, used to pose as a relative in a crisis.
advisories.reporting_route: Victims file a complaint with the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center at www.ic3.gov. The advisory also recommends a secret family word or phrase.

advisories.body: FTC Data Spotlight on gift card payment demands. Says a demand to be paid by gift card signals a scam, and that gift card payments should be reported to the card issuer right away.
advisories.says: When someone demands to be paid with a gift card, that's a scam.
advisories.reporting_route: Card issuer immediately; FTC.gov/complaint (also FTC.gov/giftcards for more information)

advisories.body: FTC press release on making complaint data more accessible, launching the first Data Spotlight. Says gift and reload cards were the top reported payment method for imposter scams, and that scammers increasingly demand gift cards, especially iTunes and Google Play.
advisories.says: Gift cards are for gifts, not for payments.
advisories.reporting_route: ftc.gov/complaint; 1-877-FTC-HELP (382-4357)

advisories.body: Singapore Police Force advisory (15 Aug 2023) on a loan-scam variant: victims see loan ads (e.g. Facebook) or get unsolicited WhatsApp messages, are sent a link to download an Android APK that is malware harvesting phone data, are then charged various fees, and are threatened with exposure of compromising photographs and harassment of their contacts if they refuse. At least nine victims lost at least $18,000 between 1 July and 13 August 2023. No mention of morphed images. Advice includes ignoring unsolicited loan offers, disabling Install Unknown App or Unknown Sources, and checking signs with the Anti-Scam Helpline.
advisories.says: Ignore such loan advertisements and do not reply to these unsolicited loans.
advisories.reporting_route: Page lists Anti-Scam Helpline 1800-722-6688 (as a place to check, not specifically to report), scamalert.sg, Police Hotline 1800-255-0000, police.gov.sg/iwitness, 999 for urgent help; report the WhatsApp number on WhatsApp and report transactions to your bank. The quote and numbers are correct, but the Helpline is for checking and information, so 'call it' overstates it.

advisories.body: News report (The News Minute, 23 Dec 2020) of an RBI caution against unauthorised digital lending apps after suicides tied to harsh recovery. RBI flagged excessive interest, hidden charges and high-handed recovery, and said platforms misuse agreements to access borrowers' phone data (the article does not list app permissions). Advice: verify the lender's background, never share KYC copies with unidentified persons, and report apps or linked bank accounts to law enforcement agencies; complaints channels are RBI's Sachet portal and cms.rbi.org.in. The RBI caution's own date is not given and the RBI release itself was not opened.
advisories.says: cautioned not to fall prey to such unscrupulous activities
advisories.reporting_route: Sachet portal (sachet.rbi.org.in) for unauthorised apps; cms.rbi.org.in for RBI-regulated entities; 'law enforcement agencies' generally. 'Local police' is not named in the article and should be dropped. The quote is correct (fuller form: 'Members of public are hereby cautioned not to fall prey to such unscrupulous activities').

advisories.body: US Federal Trade Commission consumer alert on random calls saying the recipient has won a prize.
advisories.says: if they say there's a charge to get your prize, it's a scam.
advisories.reporting_route: Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (stated on the page)

advisories.body: FBI IC3 PSA I-111523-PSA, 2023 Holiday Shopping Scams.
advisories.reporting_route: File at ic3.gov as quickly as possible; also report to the online payment service used and contact the financial institution to stop or reverse the transaction
advisories.says: Seller warning: emails claiming the buyer sent funds, without confirmation they arrived, and buyers who overpay and want the difference sent to a third party.
advisories.correct_detail: Opened. PSA number, title and date match. The quote and ic3.gov route are correct, though the route also includes reporting to the payment service and the bank.

advisories.body: Singapore Police Force advisory on phishing scams involving fake buyers on online marketplaces.
advisories.reporting_route: ScamShield app/website and 24/7 helpline 1799; report fraudulent transactions to the bank immediately; report suspicious users to the marketplace
advisories.says: Do not scan or click on dubious QR codes or URL links provided; if in doubt, contact the marketplace or delivery company directly.

advisories.body: FBI Public Service Announcement I-100322-PSA on cryptocurrency investment schemes, issued by the FBI Miami Field Office with IC3. Describes pig butchering: scammers pose as successful crypto traders, contact victims via social media or dating apps, build trust, and coach victims into continuous deposits into fake sites or apps showing fictitious returns; when victims try to withdraw they are told to pay taxes or fees.
advisories.says: Verify any investment opportunity offered by strangers or unexpected contacts on social media.
advisories.reporting_route: File a complaint at ic3.gov, including how you were first contacted, the identity given, transaction dates, payment types, amounts, wallet addresses and receiving institution details.

advisories.body: FBI IC3 (I-062424-PSA)
advisories.says: Fake law firms contact crypto-scam victims, claim to work with the FBI or CFPB, and ask for upfront fees; law enforcement does not charge fees.
advisories.reporting_route: www.ic3.gov

advisories.body: FBI IC3 (I-041825-PSA)
advisories.says: Scammers pose as IC3 employees to people who already lost money; IC3 never charges fees and never contacts individuals directly.
advisories.reporting_route: www.ic3.gov; Elder Justice Hotline 1-833-FRAUD-11 for people 60 or older

advisories.body: Singapore Police Force advisory on fund recovery services scams
advisories.says: Scammers impersonate law firms or financial companies and ask for upfront 'administrative' fees, OTPs, or remote access; at least 29 cases and S$1.2 million since Jan 2024.
advisories.reporting_route: Police hotline 1800-255-0000; Anti-Scam Helpline 1800-722-6688

advisories.body: News report (9 February 2026) quoting the ACCC acting chair ahead of Valentine's Day. More than $28.6 million lost to romance scams in 2025, up more than 20 per cent, with 1,330 reports of losses and over 80 per cent of losses from online contact. It warns never to take investment advice from an online contact. The quote and reporting route are on the opened page. This is a news report, not the ACCC page itself.
advisories.says: Do not send money, cryptocurrency or gift cards to someone you have not met in person.
advisories.reporting_route: Scamwatch (scamwatch.gov.au) and the police; contact your bank immediately if money was sent

advisories.body: Singapore Police Force advisory on cyber extortion scams involving intimate images and sexually explicit video calls. Advises avoiding explicit video calls or sharing intimate photos, not paying (payment does not ensure deletion and may lead to more extortion), stopping contact, keeping messages, screenshots and transaction records, and reporting to police.
advisories.says: The extortion often continues even after victims make payment.
advisories.reporting_route: Police report as soon as possible; ScamShield (www.scamshield.gov.sg); ScamShield Helpline 1799

advisories.body: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) public service announcement on SIM swapping: criminals move a victim's number to a SIM they control, then reset passwords and take over text-verified bank and crypto accounts.
advisories.reporting_route: Mobile carrier (immediately, to regain the number), local law enforcement, local FBI field office, and ic3.gov
advisories.says: Once the SIM is swapped, the victim's calls, texts, and other data are diverted

advisories.body: Singapore Police Force advisory (12 Nov 2025) on a new variant of WhatsApp account takeover: SMS says the account needs verifying, a link leads to a fake WhatsApp page that takes the mobile number and verification code, then fraudulent loan requests go to contacts.
advisories.reporting_route: Make a police report; call your bank immediately; contact WhatsApp for account recovery. The ScamShield Helpline 1799 is for checking doubtful messages or links, not for filing reports.
advisories.says: Beware of unusual requests received over WhatsApp, even if they were sent by your WhatsApp contacts.

advisories.body: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), public service announcement I-120324-PSA, Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud
advisories.says: Criminals use generative AI to create videos for fictitious or misleading promotional materials for investment fraud schemes.
advisories.reporting_route: File a complaint at www.ic3.gov, including identifying details, transaction details (date, payment type, amount, accounts, receiving crypto addresses) and a description of how contact began

advisories.body: Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) media release 26-157MR, 'Pump and dump scammers intensify use of fake celebrity endorsements', about fake celebrity endorsements and impersonated financial institutions
advisories.published: not stated on the page (26-157MR is a reference number; the page mentions December 2025 sentencing, so it is later)
advisories.says: For stock tips via WhatsApp, Telegram or another messaging service, 'you should assume it's a scam'; scammers lure people into messaging groups.
advisories.reporting_route: Report at Scamwatch (scamwatch.gov.au/report-a-scam); IDCARE if identity is at risk; contact the licensed platform and bank immediately if shares were bought through one

advisories.body: FBI IC3 public service announcement on work-from-home scams: fake remote jobs built on simple tasks, such as reviewing restaurants or repeatedly clicking a button; a confusing pay structure pushes victims to send cryptocurrency to the 'employer' to earn more or unlock work, and a fake interface shows growing earnings that cannot be withdrawn.
advisories.says: Never send money to an alleged employer.
advisories.reporting_route: Report to the FBI's IC3 at www.ic3.gov, including transaction details

advisories.body: Toronto Police warning (via CP24) about a 'work task' scam: victims answer a work-from-home ad, are sent to a fake rating platform, complete tasks for commissions, are told errors hurt their rating and must pay to restore it, then are asked for more payments when trying to withdraw.
advisories.says: Legitimate employers would not require staff to pay money to continue working or access wages (article's wording, may be paraphrase).
advisories.reporting_route: Toronto Police Service or Crime Stoppers (anonymous); the article does not mention the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre

advisories.body: FBI IC3 PSA I-032818-PSA, Tech Support Fraud. Covers pop-ups and locked screens, fake refund scam, advises shutting down the device, not re-contacting the scam company, and filing at ic3.gov.
advisories.says: Do not give unknown, unverified persons remote access to devices or accounts.
advisories.reporting_route: ic3.gov (file a complaint even with no loss)

advisories.body: FTC notice of 7 November 2023 on refunds to people who lost money to NTS IT Care. Pop-ups looked like OS security alerts, some falsely claiming to be from Microsoft or Apple. FTC refunding $255,000+ to 272 people.
advisories.says: The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize.
advisories.reporting_route: ReportFraud.ftc.gov

advisories.body: New Hampshire DOT warning (carried in a Union Leader story syndicated on Yahoo, dateline 21 Feb 2025) about fake texts from 'EZ-Pass' claiming an overdue toll balance, threatening excessive fees or legal action. Says similar scams have been reported by toll agencies nationwide. Advises not clicking the link and checking the account only via the official NH Turnpike E-ZPass website or app.
advisories.says: New Hampshire E-ZPass will never send text messages requesting payment for tolls with late fees.
advisories.reporting_route: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov); forward the text to 7726 (SPAM)

advisories.body: FTC consumer alert on scammers posing as utility companies; warns against one demanded payment method and says utilities generally do not take gift cards, cash reload cards or crypto.
advisories.published: 2022-06-23 (page shows this date; URL path says 2018/09)
advisories.says: Legitimate companies don't demand one specific method of payment.
advisories.reporting_route: Report to the FTC; tell the real utility; if already paid, tell the payment provider (wire or gift card company).

advisories.body: Joint Ontario utility release (Alectra, Hydro One, Hydro Ottawa, Toronto Hydro) warning of impersonation scams; fraudsters may demand prepaid debit cards, gift cards or bitcoin.
advisories.says: Utility companies will never threaten immediate disconnection for non-payment.
advisories.reporting_route: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre 1-888-495-8501 and your local utility; local police if you feel threatened (no number given on the page).
